newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Black sells stake in Australia's Fairfax group.
newsitem.headline: Black sells stake in Australia's Fairfax group.

text.p: Canadian media tycoon Conrad Black will sell his 25 percent stake in Australia's Fairfax group, which could help clear the way for billionaire Kerry Packer to take control of the country's oldest newspaper empire.

Under a deal approved by the Australian government, Black's Hollinger International Inc will sell 20 percent of John Fairfax Holdings Ltd. to New Zealand's Brierley Investments Ltd. for A$447.1 million ($353.2 million), Brierley said on Monday.
Brierley said it also had a conditional agreement to purchase the remaining five percent stake held for another A$106.7 million ($84.3 million), subject to Fairfax shareholders approval.
Brierley is an investment group based in Auckland, New Zealand, noted for taking strategic stakes in companies and then selling at a profit.
Analysts said they did not expect it to be a long-term Fairfax shareholder.
They pointed out that Packer, Australia's richest man, would not be able to launch a bid for Fairfax unless a government inquiry led to changes in Australian media cross-ownership regulations.

Packer, who has close relations with the government, holds 15 percent of Fairfax and is not allowed to raise that stake because of his television holdings, although his Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd. has said it would like to merge with Fairfax.
The Fairfax group was founded 165 years ago and became one of Australia's big newspaper empires with flagship titles such as the Sydney Morning Herald and The Melbourne Age.

But it went into receivership in 1990 with debts of A$1.20 billion ($94.8 million) after a younger scion of the Fairfax family made a failed A$2.25 billion ($1.78 billion) bid to take the then-listed company private.

The group was subsequently rescued under a deal engineered by Black that saw 80 percent of it floated and left him with a 15 percent stake, later raised to 25 percent, held through his London-based subsidiary that publishes The Daily Telegraph.
Fairfax has been the subject of much ownership speculation with Black, News Corp.'s Rupert Murdoch and Packer all variously building up stakes in recent years.
The situation has been muddied by government rules, currently under review, on foreign and cross-media ownership. News Corp. sold off its stake, which was just below five percent, last month.
Hollinger said the sale of its Fairfax stake was prompted by suggestions that the Australian government would not review foreign ownership limits in the media sector.

"For several years, Telegraph and Hollinger International have repeatedly stated that the existing ambiguous foreign ownership rules in Australia were creating an extremely difficult environment for Fairfax to work in and we were not prepared to keep the place of the most influential shareholder in Fairfax warm for whomever may seize it under existing media ownership rules," Black said in a statement.
One Australian media analyst said Black was also coming under pressure from his U.S. shareholders to do something with the Fairfax stake.
Brierley executive director Rod Price said the company expected to be an active long-term shareholder in Fairfax, not just a strategic buyer.

"Those perceptions are good to write about but in fact they are not really part of what happens," Price told Reuters. "I don't think you have seen a fair reflection of what the underlying earnings can be in this company."
